catalog_quote: Although prosodic features are not directly marked in either Tocharian language, the position of the Tocharian B stress accent can be inferred from the behavior of the central vowels /a/ and /ə/. These, as is well known, have the relatively low allophones [a] <ā> and [ʌ] <a> under the accent and the relatively high allophones [ʌ] <a> and [ɨ] <ä> when unaccented. Alternations of the type lákle (< *lä́-) 'sorrow': pl. läklénta, ā́ke 'end' : pl. akénta (< *āk-´), etc. are the foundation of Krause and Thomas' "basic rule" of Toch. B accentuation: "In den meisten zweisilbigen Wörtern ruht der Akzent auf der ersten, in drei- (und teilweise vier-)silbigen auf der zweiten Silbe" (Krause and Thomas 1960: 43). Many exceptions have been noted to this rule, some of them easily explained. The numerous disyllabic Toch. B forms with second-syllable accent, for example (e.g., akā́lk 'wish', ñäktéṃts 'g…
sweep_summary: Two Glottolog title hits, both De Gruyter Festschrift chapters and both closed: Ringe 1987 'On the prehistory of Tocharian B accent' (DOI 10.1515/9783110853223.254; diachronic, per Jasanoff 2015 n. 7 an elaboration of Marggraf 1970 on accent-conditioned epenthesis; priority low) and Adams 2003a 'Patterns of stress and rhythm in Tocharian B prosody' (DOI 10.1515/9783110897722.1; CEToM record verified, pp. 1-12 in Bauer & Pinault eds., TLSM 144; its only citer and Adams's 2013 sequel are verse-metrics papers, so its frame is metrical; priority medium). Unpaywall, Semantic Scholar, CORE, fatcat, OpenAlex, DASH and archive.org show no open copy; De Gruyter, Google Books (partial views OVkjAAAAQBAJ and q_WhLdCr3UEC), HathiTrust (mdp.39015051440710, search-only) and the Richmond repository all returned bot challenges by automated download, and the web search and Google Books API budgets were exhausted. Read this search of works with stress in the title: Bross, Ryan & Gunkel 2014 (open DASH preprint, verse colometry, silent on word stress) and the Burlak & Itkin 2013 Tocharian B chapter from the open Jazyki mira volume already held by the project (p. 446: majority penultimate stress, causative-initial and loan-final exceptions, rules 'not exactly known'), which refines but does not overturn the catalog's fixed-unreviewed coding resting on Jasanoff 2015 and Krause & Thomas 1960 (both held and read in the earlier reading).

new_statements.quote: В Т.B.я. реконструируется разноместное подвижное динамическое ударение русского типа, определяющее фонетическую и графическую реализацию гласных среднего ряда. Правила постановки ударения в точности неизвестны, имеется очень много примеров акцентных колебаний. В большинстве слов оно падает на второй слог от конца, но в ряде случаев это не так. В частности, в формах каузатива ударным, как правило, является первый слог, например: tsálpästär ... śársäṣṣäṃ ...; в некоторых заимствованиях — последний, например: akā́lk ‛желание’ < бактр. αγαλγο.
new_statements.translation: For Tocharian B a free-position, mobile, dynamic stress of the Russian type is reconstructed, which determines the phonetic and graphic realisation of the central-row vowels. The rules of stress placement are not known exactly; there are very many examples of accentual fluctuation. In most words it falls on the second syllable from the end, but in a number of cases this is not so. In particular, in causative forms the first syllable is as a rule stressed, e.g. tsálpästär ... śársäṣṣäṃ ...; in some loanwords the last, e.g. akā́lk 'wish' < Bactrian αγαλγο.
new_statements.citation: Burlak, S. A. & I. B. Itkin. 2013. 'Тохарский B язык'. In Языки мира: Реликтовые индоевропейские языки Передней и Центральной Азии, 444-485. Moscow: Academia.
new_statements.reading: A modern reference-survey statement: majority penultimate stress, with morphologically conditioned (causative-initial) and lexically conditioned (loan-final, certain compounds) exceptions, and an explicit caveat that the system is 'free/mobile' and the rules not fully known. It agrees with the catalog's positional ('fixed') majority rule while formulating it as penultimate rather than Krause & Thomas 1960's syllable-count rule; the two formulations differ only for words of four or more syllables, where K&T themselves (p. 45 Anm. 2) say no sure rules can be given.
new_statements.check: quotation verified in source (minor differences in wording)

audit.reasoning: (1) Quote check: the deciding Jasanoff 2015 p. 87 passage, the p. 90 rules, and the Tocharian Online sec. 1.4 domain quote are all verbatim in the copies we hold at the stated places. I also downloaded the primary Krause & Thomas 1960 Elementarbuch from archive.org and confirmed the Grundregel first-hand at sec. 10 p. 43 ('Die Hauptregel lautet: In den meisten zweisilbigen Wörtern ruht der Akzent auf der ersten, in drei- (und teilweise vier)silbigen auf der zweiten Silbe'), with K&T's own exception list (causative -sk- presents initial-accented despite trisyllabicity; causative pret. II; subj. V / oy-opt; clitic-like words under weak sentence accent) matching Jasanoff's classes 1-2, and the 'bewegliches -o' account of end-accented disyllables matching our the primary-stress rule note. (2) Deciding source: a 2015 specialist phonology article on exactly this question quoting the standard reference grammar
